title: EagleDepth: Efficient Fine-Grained Depth Estimation via Pixel Diffusion Decoder

paper.title: EagleDepth: Efficient Fine-Grained Depth Estimation via Pixel Diffusion Decoder
paper.abstract: Abstract Recovering detailed geometry from high-resolution images is critical for precise perception of the surroundings and objects. However, existing methods which use latent-space modeling and VAE reconstruction can compromise geometric details. Furthermore, decoding from latent codes introduces substantial inference overhead. To address those issues, we present EagleDepth , an efficient framework for high-resolution monocular depth estimation that combines the geometric priors of latent diffusion with fine-grained pixel-space generation. Our key idea is to retain depth-aware latent representations as guidance while generating the final depth map directly in pixel space. We train the latent and pixel components sequentially: first, we fine-tune a pretrained latent diffusion model using paired RGB–depth supervision; then, we adapt a pretrained pixel diffusion decoder, PiD, to predict depth conditioned on the learned features. Training of the pixel component starts at 1024 resolution and continues across multiple resolutions up to 4K. The latent branch processes resized, lower-resolution RGB images, while the pixel branch generates depth at the target resolution, bypassing the original VAE decoder. This design preserves learned geometric knowledge without requiring the latent backbone to operate at the output resolution. On five commonly used depth estimation datasets and the high-resolution Synth4K dataset, our framework achieves state-of-the-art depth estimation performance, with faster inference and better preservation of fine structures and object boundaries.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Monocular depth estimation provides a fundamental capability for robotic navigation ( Redder et al., 2025 ; Gode et al., 2025 ) , manipulation ( Zhang et al., 2026c ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) , and 3D scene understanding ( Eigen et al., 2014 ; Ouyang et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2024 ) . Modern cameras capture multi-megapixel images containing small objects, thin structures, and closely spaced boundaries, creating a demand for depth predictions that preserve geometric detail at comparable resolutions. However, representative generative depth and geometry estimators are trained at resolutions such as 512 × 512 512\times 512 and 1024 × 768 1024\times 768 pixels ( Xu et al., 2026a ; Xu et al., 2026b ) . Downsampling images to these working resolutions can weaken or eliminate visual cues associated with small structures. Efficiently recovering high-resolution, fine-grained geometry is therefore important for applications such as small-obstacle avoidance and precise robotic manipulation. Preserving local detail and global scene consistency at high resolution requires careful control of computational cost. Interpolation cannot recover unresolved structures, while increasing the working resolution raises computation and memory demands. Methods such as PatchFusion ( Li et al., 2024 ) and PatchRefiner ( Li et al., 2026 ) refine local patches using global image context to recover detailed, coherent depth maps. For diffusion models, iterative denoising can further increase inference costs, particularly when processing large spatial grids. Generative methods ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2024 ) such as Marigold ( Ke et al., 2024b ) demonstrate that pretrained latent diffusion models can acquire depth-specific knowledge through paired RGB–depth supervision. These representations help resolve ambiguity by providing learned geometric context when visual evidence is incomplete. However, latent compression can obscure narrow structures and closely spaced boundaries, while reconstruction with a variational autoencoder (VAE) can introduce additional geometric errors. Boundary degradation occurs even when reconstructing encoded ground-truth geometry ( Xu et al., 2026a ; Xu et al., 2026b ) . Moreover, the decoder must reconstruct the full-resolution output, adding computation as image size increases. These limitations motivate retaining useful latent priors without the original reconstruction pathway. Pixel-space diffusion avoids VAE reconstruction by generating geometric outputs directly. Pixel-Perfect Depth ( Xu et al., 2026a ) predicts depth using pretrained image encoders such as Depth Anything V2, while PointDiT ( Xu et al., 2026b ) generates dense 3D point maps conditioned on frozen DINOv3 image features. However, processing high-resolution spatial representations remains computationally demanding as the number of spatial tokens increases, and iterative sampling can further increase latency. Direct pixel-space generation therefore still faces the challenge of recovering fine geometry efficiently at multi-megapixel resolutions. We introduce EagleDepth , a framework that combines depth-adapted latent representations with direct pixel-space prediction. Our key idea is to separate geometric prior extraction from high-resolution detail recovery to allocate computation across different resolutions. The latent branch supplies depth-aware guidance at low resolution, while the original RGB image provides the local evidence needed to resolve fine structures. We adapt the pretrained Pixel Diffusion Decoder (PiD) ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , originally designed to jointly decode and upsample image latents. Depth-specific supervision adapts this formulation to geometric prediction, where details must reflect meaningful surfaces and depth discontinuities rather than visual sharpness alone. We train the two components sequentially. First, we fine-tune FLUX.2-klein-4B ( Black Forest Labs, 2026 ) , a pretrained latent diffusion model, on paired RGB–depth data. This branch processes resized, lower-resolution RGB images to provide depth-aware guidance. We then freeze this branch and fine-tune PiD, conditioned on its guidance and the original RGB image. Pixel training starts with approximately 1024 2 1024^{2} pixels per image and continues across multiple resolutions up to 4K. The pixel branch directly generates target-resolution depth, bypassing the original VAE decoder during inference without scaling the latent backbone to the output resolution. We evaluate this design on six benchmark datasets, including the high-resolution Synth4K dataset, covering standard depth estimation and high-resolution prediction up to 4K. EagleDepth achieves state-of-the-art depth estimation performance, with better preservation of fine structures and object boundaries, together with faster inference. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We introduce EagleDepth , a generative monocular depth estimator that brings together the geometric knowledge of depth-adapted latent diffusion and the pixel-space modeling capabilities for efficient, detailed prediction at high resolutions. • We show that depth-aware features from downsampled RGB inputs can guide depth generation at higher resolutions. This enables our framework to retain latent geometric priors without executing the latent backbone at the output resolution or using its VAE decoder. • Experiments on five commonly used depth estimation datasets and the high-resolution Synth4K dataset establish state-of-the-art depth estimation results for our 1024-resolution model and its multi-resolution extension supporting resolutions up to 4K, with consistent improvements in fine-structure recovery and boundary fidelity, alongside faster inference.

sections.heading: 2.1 Monocular Depth Estimation
sections.text: Discriminative approaches such as DPT ( Ranftl et al., 2021 ) and Depth Anything V2 ( Yang et al., 2024 ) directly predict depth using pretrained visual representations, while PatchFusion ( Li et al., 2024 ) extends depth estimation to high resolutions through patch-based fusion. Generative approaches leverage priors learned from image synthesis: Marigold ( Ke et al., 2024b ) and Lotus-G ( He et al., 2025b ) adapt pretrained latent diffusion models for depth prediction. To address geometric artifacts associated with latent reconstruction, Pixel-Perfect Depth ( Xu et al., 2026a ) directly generates depth maps in pixel space, while PointDiT ( Xu et al., 2026b ) applies pixel-space diffusion to dense 3D point maps. These methods demonstrate the value of pretrained representations and direct geometric generation, although efficiently recovering fine-grained geometry at multi-megapixel resolutions remains challenging. Our approach combines these strengths by using depth-adapted features from a lower-resolution latent backbone to guide depth generation at the target resolution.

sections.heading: 2.2 Diffusion Models
sections.text: Latent diffusion models ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Zhou et al., 2022 ) reduce generative modeling costs by operating in compressed representations and reconstructing outputs through pretrained autoencoders. Although computationally effective, this formulation makes output fidelity dependent on latent compression and reconstruction. Recent advances revisit diffusion directly in pixel space. JiT ( Li and He, 2026 ) demonstrates effective clean-image prediction with plain transformers, while PixelDiT ( Yu et al., 2026b ) combines patch-level and pixel-level processing for efficient pixel-space generation. Complementing these approaches, PiD ( Lu et al., 2026 ) introduces a latent-conditioned pixel diffusion decoder that jointly performs decoding and spatial upsampling, replacing conventional VAE decoding. We build on this pretrained decoder and adapt it from image synthesis to monocular depth estimation. Specifically, depth-aware features learned through latent diffusion adaptation condition pixel-space depth generation, allowing us to reuse pretrained generative knowledge for efficient, high-resolution geometric prediction.

sections.heading: 3.2 Framework Overview
sections.text: We aim to produce detailed, high-resolution depth maps, which requires capturing both scene-wide depth relationships and fine local geometry. Pretrained latent diffusion models combine rich visual priors with compact latent-space modeling. However, spatial compression and autoencoder reconstruction can lose fine details, and high-resolution VAE decoding incurs substantial computational and memory overhead. To address these limitations, we draw on the fine-detail modeling capabilities of pixel diffusion. Specifically, we adapt a pixel diffusion decoder pretrained for image synthesis, PiD ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , to decode coarse depth latents predicted by a depth-adapted latent diffusion model. During decoding, the pixel model uses high-resolution RGB observations to recover depth details beyond the coarse representation, producing a detailed depth map at the target resolution. Figure 2 illustrates the overall framework of our proposed method. Given a high-resolution RGB image 𝒙 rgb H ∈ ℝ H × W × 3 \bm{x}_{\mathrm{rgb}}^{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} , we resize it to a lower resolution (i.e., 512 2 512^{2} pixels in total) and encode it using the pretrained autoencoder encoder ℰ \mathcal{E} . Our pixel decoder backbone, PiD, builds on a pixel diffusion PixelDiT ( Yu et al., 2026b ) , which uses diffusion transformer (DiT) blocks to process patch-level features and pixel transformer (PiT) blocks to refine pixel-level details. This coarse-to-fine design enables efficient high-resolution depth prediction with accurate scene-level structure and fine geometric detail.

sections.heading: 3.3 Adapting Latent Diffusion for Coarse Depth Prediction
sections.text: Accurate coarse depth provides reliable geometric guidance for subsequent detail refinement, motivating us to improve the accuracy of the latent depth predictor. Prior works have established effective strategies for adapting pretrained generative models to depth estimation ( Ke et al., 2024a ; He et al., 2025a ; He et al., 2025b ) . Motivated by these findings, we adopt deterministic single-step prediction and replace noise inputs with encoded RGB images. We use FLUX.2-klein-4B ( Black Forest Labs, 2026 ) , a pretrained rectified-flow transformer, as our backbone to balance model capability and computational efficiency. To improve accuracy, we revisit the supervision objective for the latent predictor. Conventional latent flow matching trains models to predict instantaneous velocities in latent space. However, flow trajectories are not necessarily straight, so even accurate instantaneous velocities may yield endpoint errors in a single-step update ( Frans et al., 2025 ) . Moreover, although latent-space supervision encourages predictions to match targets, the decoder may still amplify small residual errors. Thus, latent-space supervision may be suboptimal. Since our single-step formulation does not require iterative latent-space sampling, we can directly supervise the decoded depth map: 𝒙 ^ depth L = Π ⁡ [ 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝒛 ^ depth L ) ] , ℒ coarse = ℒ depth ​ ( 𝒙 ^ depth L , 𝒙 depth L ) , \hat{\bm{x}}_{\mathrm{depth}}^{L}=\Pi\!\left[\mathcal{D}\!\left(\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mathrm{depth}}^{L}\right)\right],\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{coarse}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{depth}}\!\left(\hat{\bm{x}}_{\mathrm{depth}}^{L},\bm{x}_{\mathrm{depth}}^{L}\right), (5) where 𝒟 \mathcal{D} denotes the VAE decoder, Π \Pi averages the output channels, 𝒙 depth L \bm{x}_{\mathrm{depth}}^{L} is the normalized low-resolution ground-truth depth, and ℒ depth \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{depth}} denotes the loss used for depth supervision. We freeze the decoder and backpropagate the depth loss through it, training the latent predictor under a fixed decoding mapping. This objective evaluates the quality of latent predictions by the accuracy of their decoded depth maps, encouraging accurate depth values and geometric structure.

sections.heading: 3.4 Decoding Fine-Grained Depth with Pixel Diffusion
sections.text: Central to our approach is adapting a pretrained pixel diffusion decoder to depth estimation. Compared with a conventional VAE decoder trained for reconstruction, a pixel diffusion decoder provides a generative prior learned in pixel space that can help recover fine details beyond the coarse latent representation. Specifically, we build upon PiD ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , which formulates latent decoding as latent-conditioned image generation in pixel space. While the original model decodes natural-image latents, we fine-tune it to decode the predicted coarse depth latents into detailed, high-resolution depth maps using the high-resolution RGB input, as described in Section 3.2 . Following prior findings on pixel-space diffusion ( Li and He, 2026 ) , we use direct clean-sample prediction (x-pred). To initialize the x-pred decoder from PiD’s pretrained velocity model, we negate the weights and bias of its final linear layer: the negated velocity target, − 𝒖 t = 𝒙 0 − ϵ -\bm{u}_{t}=\bm{x}_{0}-\bm{\epsilon} , differs from the clean-sample target 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} only by a noise term. The unpatchification head in diffusion transformers maps each patch token to a p × p p\times p pixel block without local spatial mixing, leaving discontinuities along patch boundaries. In depth maps, these artifacts can be especially noticeable at object boundaries, where one patch spans sharply different depths. Convolutions can mitigate these inconsistencies through local feature fusion ( He et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . However, the large patch size in pixel diffusion makes it costly for convolutional heads to capture patch-wide context after unpatchification. We therefore insert a continuity-promoting module before the original output projection, interleaving progressive unpatchification with small-kernel convolutions to mix hidden features at multiple spatial scales. Specifically, given the normalized hidden features 𝒉 ( 0 ) \bm{h}^{(0)} , the module progressively unfolds their within-patch dimensions into the spatial grid and applies convolutions after each unfolding step: 𝒉 ( k + 1 ) = Conv 3 × 3 ( GELU ( Conv 3 × 3 ( Unpatchify 2 × 2 ( 𝒉 ( k ) ) ) ) ) , k = 0 , … , log 2 p − 1 . \bm{h}^{(k+1)}=\operatorname{Conv}_{3\times 3}\!\left(\operatorname{GELU}\!\left(\operatorname{Conv}_{3\times 3}\!\left(\operatorname{Unpatchify}_{2\times 2}\!\left(\bm{h}^{(k)}\right)\right)\right)\right),\quad k=0,\ldots,\log_{2}p-1. (6) Each step doubles the spatial grid dimensions until the full pixel resolution is reached. The original linear projection is then applied to produce the output. Each Conv–GELU–Conv block is jointly initialized to implement an identity mapping, preserving the pretrained readout at initialization.

sections.heading: 3.5 Training Strategy
sections.text: We train the two components sequentially. First, we adapt the latent diffusion model for coarse depth prediction at approximately 512 2 512^{2} pixels, learning to provide reliable scene-level geometry for subsequent detail refinement. We then freeze this model and fine-tune PiD at approximately 1024 2 1024^{2} pixels, adapting its pretrained generative prior to decode the predicted depth latents and recover fine geometric details with RGB guidance. This yields our Ours (1024) variant. RGB MoGe-2 PPD InfiniDepth Ours Figure 3: Qualitative comparison with leading monocular depth estimation methods. Our method preserves fine geometric details and thin structures while maintaining sharp depth boundaries and smooth surfaces, as highlighted by the arrows and zoomed-in regions. To further extend the model’s high-resolution capability, we continue training PiD with mixed resolutions up to 4K. During this training, 25% of batches follow the same 1024 2 1024^{2} data settings as before, while the remaining 75% are drawn exclusively from high-resolution datasets across multiple resolution buckets. Retaining the 1024 2 1024^{2} training distribution helps preserve the model’s existing capability as it learns to recover details at higher resolutions. This mixed-resolution training yields our Ours (MR) variant. Throughout PiD training, the latent model remains frozen and processes inputs at approximately 512 2 512^{2} pixels regardless of PiD’s output resolution, while its predicted latents are resized to the target patch grid before injection into PiD. Both components are optimized using an L1 loss, a gradient matching loss ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , and a virtual normal loss ( Yin et al., 2019 ) , with respective weights of 1 1 , 2 2 , and 0.5 0.5 .

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Datasets. Our model is trained on 536K RGB–depth pairs sampled from several datasets: Hypersim ( Roberts et al., 2021 ) , VKITTI2 ( Cabon et al., 2020 ) , TartanAir ( Wang et al., 2020 ) , IRS ( Wang et al., 2021 ) , EDEN ( Le et al., 2021 ) , RobbyReal ( Tan et al., 2026 ) , UnrealStereo4K ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) , UrbanSyn ( Gómez et al., 2025 ) , Spring ( Mehl et al., 2023 ) , and Rawmantic3D ( Team, 2026 ) . Only the last four datasets are used as high-resolution training dataset. We evaluate depth estimation performance on five real-world benchmarks: NYUv2 ( Silberman et al., 2012 ) , KITTI ( Geiger et al., 2012 ) , ETH3D ( Schops et al., 2017 ) , ScanNet ( Dai et al., 2017 ) , and DIODE ( Vasiljevic et al., 2019 ) . To further assess high-resolution prediction and fine-detail recovery, we use Synth4K ( Yu et al., 2026a ) , a synthetic high-resolution benchmark that comprises five subsets. Implementation details. We transform the ground-truth depth into log space via log ⁡ ( 1 + d ) \log(1+d) and normalize each depth map to − 1 , 1 -1,1 using its 2nd and 98th percentiles. We adapt FLUX.2-klein-4B ( Labs, 2025 ) with rank-256 LoRA for 30,000 steps at a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} . With the latent model frozen, we fully fine-tune PiD ( Lu et al., 2026 ) at approximately 1024 2 1024^{2} pixels for 50,000 steps with a learning rate of 3 × 10 − 5 3\times 10^{-5} , obtaining Ours (1024). Mixed-resolution training continues for another 20,000 steps with the learning rate reduced to 10 − 5 10^{-5} , producing Ours (MR). All models are trained on 8 NVIDIA GPUs, using the AdamW optimizer and a total batch size of 16. Evaluation protocol. We evaluate all comparison methods under the same resolution settings for fair comparisons. Specifically, images from the five real-world benchmarks are resized to approximately 1024 2 1024^{2} pixels with aspect ratios preserved, whereas Synth4K is evaluated at native 4K resolution. We report AbsRel and δ 1 \delta_{1} to assess overall depth accuracy. For datasets with dense ground-truth depth, we further report HF-masked AbsRel and δ 1 \delta_{1} ( Yu et al., 2026a ) and boundary F1-score ( r = 1 r=1 ) ( Bochkovskiy et al., 2025 ) to assess fine-detail recovery in the predicted depth maps.

sections.heading: 4.2 Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods
sections.text: We compare EagleDepth with several leading methods for depth estimation, including: MiDaS ( Ranftl et al., 2020 ) , DA2 ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , Marigold ( Ke et al., 2024b ) , Lotus-2 ( He et al., 2025a ) , DA3 ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , MoGe-2 ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , PPD ( Xu et al., 2026a ) , PointDiT ( Xu et al., 2026b ) , InfiniDepth ( Yu et al., 2026a ) , and URGT ( Cui et al., 2026 ) , where the last two methods are designed for high-resolution depth prediction. Qualitative results. We present visual comparisons across diverse scenes and image resolutions in Figure 3 . EagleDepth consistently captures the overall scene structure while preserving local geometric details. Compared with other methods, our model more faithfully recovers fine structures and delineates object boundaries that are otherwise blurred or lost. These visual improvements agree with the gains in HF-masked accuracy and boundary F1, supporting the effectiveness of combining coarse depth guidance with RGB-guided pixel decoding across scenes and resolutions. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented EagleDepth , a framework that combines depth-adapted latent diffusion with pixel diffusion for efficient fine-grained depth estimation. The latent branch predicts coarse depth latents from downsampled RGB inputs, while the pixel branch generates depth directly at the target resolution conditioned on these latents. This design retains learned geometric priors while reducing detail loss from latent-space modeling and VAE reconstruction. It also avoids the substantial overhead of VAE decoding at high resolutions. We train two variants: one at approximately 1024 2 1024^{2} pixels and a mixed-resolution extension supporting prediction up to 4K ( 2160 × 3840 2160\times 3840 ). Experiments on five commonly used depth estimation datasets and Synth4K demonstrate strong overall accuracy and better preservation of fine structures and object boundaries.

sections.heading: A.1 Latent backbone: FLUX.2
sections.text: We use FLUX.2-klein-4B ( Labs, 2025 ) as the latent backbone. This pretrained rectified-flow transformer contains approximately four billion parameters, with five double-stream blocks followed by twenty single-stream blocks. All blocks use a hidden dimension of 3072 and 24 attention heads. The double-stream blocks maintain separate image and text projections and feed-forward networks, while jointly attending to tokens from both modalities. The single-stream blocks process the concatenated sequence of image and text tokens with parallel attention and feed-forward branches. The backbone uses query and key normalization, rotary positional embeddings, and timestep-conditioned feature modulation. Its Qwen3-4B text encoder concatenates features from three intermediate layers into 7680-dimensional text tokens, which are projected to the transformer width. The accompanying FLUX.2 autoencoder uses a convolutional encoder–decoder with residual blocks and a 32-channel latent representation at one-eighth of the image height and width. Packing each 2 × 2 2\times 2 latent neighborhood into the channel dimension produces 128-channel features at a spatial stride of 16. The encoder uses the posterior mean and normalizes the packed features using fixed pretrained channel statistics. For an input image of size H × W H\times W , the resulting latent representation has spatial dimensions H / 16 × W / 16 H/16\times W/16 and 128 channels. The transformer predicts a velocity in this same representation. We initialize the latent predictor from the released distilled checkpoint and adapt its transformer blocks with rank-256 LoRA. The encoded RGB image serves as the input state at t ⋆ = 0.5 t^{\star}=0.5 , and the depth latent is obtained by the single flow update in Eq. 3 . For text conditioning, we use the fixed prompt “A dense grayscale monocular depth map of the scene, far surfaces brighter and near surfaces darker.” Its embedding is computed once and cached. The autoencoder remains frozen; its decoder is used for the coarse-depth supervision described in the main paper. During pixel adaptation and final inference, the latent predictor remains frozen and operates at approximately 512 2 512^{2} input pixels, passing its predicted depth latent directly to the pixel diffusion decoder.

sections.heading: A.2 Pixel backbone: PiD
sections.text: We use pretrained PiD ( Lu et al., 2026 ) as the pixel backbone, adopting its FLUX.2-compatible v1.5 architecture. Built on PixelDiT ( Yu et al., 2026b ) , PiD combines a patch transformer with a pixel pathway to jointly perform latent decoding and spatial upsampling. The patch transformer processes 16 × 16 16\times 16 image patches using 14 MM-DiT blocks with hidden dimension 1536 and 24 attention heads, allowing image and text tokens to interact through joint attention. The pixel pathway uses two PiT blocks with 16-dimensional pixel features, conditioned on the patch representations through adaptive normalization. Each PiT block compresses the features within each patch for attention across patches, then expands them back for pixel updates. A convolutional adapter maps the conditioning latent to features aligned with the image patch grid. For FLUX.2 latents, the packed 128-channel representation is first unpacked into 32 channels and resized by nearest-neighbor interpolation to H / p × W / p H/p\times W/p , where p = 16 p=16 . sections.text: To improve training efficiency and reduce storage requirements, we filter and subsample the larger training datasets. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.04554v1 [cs.CV] 03 Oct 2026 EagleDepth: Efficient Fine-Grained Depth Estimation via Pixel Diffusion Decoder Bowen Chai 1∗ , Tianbao Zhang 1∗ , Shuyu Wu 1 , Dexin Zuo 1 , Zhaoxin Fan 2 , Danping Zou 1† 1 Shanghai Jiao Tong University 2 Beihang University Project Page: sjtu-visys-team.github.io/EagleDepth/ Abstract Recovering detailed geometry from high-resolution images is critical for precise perception of the surroundings and objects. However, existing methods which use latent-space modeling and VAE reconstruction can compromise geometric details. Furthermore, decoding from latent codes introduces substantial inference overhead. To address those issues, we present EagleDepth , an efficient framework for high-resolution monocular depth estimation that combines the geometric priors of latent diffusion with fine-grained pixel-space generation. Our key idea is to retain depth-aware latent representations as guidance while generating the final depth map directly in pixel space. We train the latent and pixel components sequentially: first, we fine-tune a pretrained latent diffusion model using paired RGB–depth supervision; then, we adapt a pretrained pixel diffusion decoder, PiD, to predict depth conditioned on the learned features. Training of the pixel component starts at 1024 resolution and continues across multiple resolutions up to 4K. The latent branch processes resized, lower-resolution RGB images, while the pixel branch generates depth at the target resolution, bypassing the original VAE decoder. This design preserves learned geometric knowledge without requiring the latent backbone to operate at the output resolution. On five commonly used depth estimation datasets and the high-resolution Synth4K dataset, our framework achieves state-of-the-art depth estimation performance, with faster inference and better preservation of fine structures and object boundaries. 1 1 footnotetext: Equal contribution. † \dagger Corresponding author: Danping Zou, dpzou@sjtu.edu.cn. Figure 1: EagleDepth excels at predicting fine-grained depth maps from high-resolution images. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, our model achieves better depth estimation results with faster inference, as shown in the radar chart (quality metrics averaged over the five Synth4K ( Yu et al., 2026a ) subsets; larger radii indicate better performance) 1 Introduction Monocular depth estimation provides a fundamental capability for robotic navigation ( Redder et al., 2025 ; Gode et al., 2025 ) , manipulation ( Zhang et al., 2026c ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) , and 3D scene understanding ( Eigen et al., 2014 ; Ouyang et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2024 ) . Modern cameras capture multi-megapixel images containing small objects, thin structures, and closely spaced boundaries, creating a demand for depth predictions that preserve geometric detail at comparable resolutions. However, representative generative depth and geometry estimators are trained at resolutions such as 512 × 512 512\times 512 and 1024 × 768 1024\times 768 pixels ( Xu et al., 2026a ; Xu et al., 2026b ) . Downsampling images to these working resolutions can weaken or eliminate visual cues associated with small structures. Efficiently recovering high-resolution, fine-grained geometry is therefore important for applications such as small-obstacle avoidance and precise robotic manipulation. Preserving local detail and global scene consistency at high resolution requires careful control of computational cost. Interpolation cannot recover unresolved structures, while increasing the working resolution raises computation and memory demands. Methods such as PatchFusion ( Li et al., 2024 ) and PatchRefiner ( Li et al., 2026 ) refine local patches using global image context to recover detailed, coherent depth maps. For diffusion models, iterative denoising can further increase inference costs, particularly when processing large spatial grids. Generative methods ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2024 ) such as Marigold ( Ke et al., 2024b ) demonstrate that pretrained latent diffusion models can acquire depth-specific knowledge through paired RGB–depth supervision. These representations help resolve ambiguity by providing learned geometric context when visual evidence is incomplete. However, latent compression can obscure narrow structures and closely spaced boundaries, while reconstruction with a variational autoencoder (VAE) can introduce additional geometric errors. Boundary degradation occurs even when reconstructing encoded ground-truth geometry ( Xu et al., 2026a ; Xu et al., 2026b ) . Moreover, the decoder must reconstruct the full-resolution output, adding computation as image size increases. These limitations motivate retaining useful latent priors without the original reconstruction pathway. Pixel-space diffusion avoids VAE reconstruction by generating geometric outputs directly. Pixel-Perfect Depth ( Xu et al., 2026a ) predicts depth using pretrained image encoders such as Depth Anything V2, while PointDiT ( Xu et al., 2026b ) generates dense 3D point maps conditioned on frozen DINOv3 image features. However, processing high-resolution spatial representations remains computationally demanding as the number of spatial tokens increases, and iterative sampling can further increase latency. Direct pixel-space generation therefore still faces the challenge of recovering fine geometry efficiently at multi-megapixel resolutions. We introduce EagleDepth , a framework that combines depth-adapted latent representations with direct pixel-space prediction. Our key idea is to separate geometric prior extraction from high-resolution detail recovery to allocate computation across different resolutions. The latent branch supplies depth-aware guidance at low resolution, while the original RGB image provides the local evidence needed to resolve fine structures. We adapt the pretrained Pixel Diffusion Decoder (PiD) ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , originally designed to jointly decode and upsample image latents. Depth-specific supervision adapts this formulation to geometric prediction, where details must reflect meaningful surfaces and depth discontinuities rather than visual sharpness alone. We train the two components sequentially. First, we fine-tune FLUX.2-klein-4B ( Black Forest Labs, 2026 ) , a pretrained latent diffusion model, on paired RGB–depth data. This branch processes resized, lower-resolution RGB images to provide depth-aware guidance. We then freeze this branch and fine-tune PiD, conditioned on its guidance and the original RGB image. Pixel training starts with approximately 1024 2 1024^{2} pixels per image and continues across multiple resolutions up to 4K. The pixel branch directly generates target-resolution depth, bypassing the original VAE decoder during inference without scaling the latent backbone to the output resolution. We evaluate this design on six benchmark datasets, including the high-resolution Synth4K dataset, covering standard depth estimation and high-resolution prediction up to 4K. EagleDepth achieves state-of-the-art depth estimation performance, with better preservation of fine structures and object boundaries, together with faster inference. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We introduce EagleDepth , a generative monocular depth estimator that brings together the geometric knowledge of depth-adapted latent diffusion and the pixel-space modeling capabilities for efficient, detailed prediction at high resolutions. • We show that depth-aware features from downsampled RGB inputs can guide depth generation at higher resolutions. This enables our framework to retain latent geometric priors without executing the latent backbone at the output resolution or using its VAE decoder. • Experiments on five commonly used depth estimation datasets and the high-resolution Synth4K dataset establish state-of-the-art depth estimation results for our 1024-resolution model and its multi-resolution extension supporting resolutions up to 4K, with consistent improvements in fine-structure recovery and boundary fidelity, alongside faster inference. 2 Related Work 2.1 Monocular Depth Estimation Discriminative approaches such as DPT ( Ranftl et al., 2021 ) and Depth Anything V2 ( Yang et al., 2024 ) directly predict depth using pretrained visual representations, while PatchFusion ( Li et al., 2024 ) extends depth estimation to high resolutions through patch-based fusion. Generative approaches leverage priors learned from image synthesis: Marigold ( Ke et al., 2024b ) and Lotus-G ( He et al., 2025b ) adapt pretrained latent diffusion models for depth prediction. To address geometric artifacts associated with latent reconstruction, Pixel-Perfect Depth ( Xu et al., 2026a ) directly generates depth maps in pixel space, while PointDiT ( Xu et al., 2026b ) applies pixel-space diffusion to dense 3D point maps. These methods demonstrate the value of pretrained representations and direct geometric generation, although efficiently recovering fine-grained geometry at multi-megapixel resolutions remains challenging. Our approach combines these strengths by using depth-adapted features from a lower-resolution latent backbone to guide depth generation at the target resolution. 2.2 Diffusion Models Latent diffusion models ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Zhou et al., 2022 ) reduce generative modeling costs by operating in compressed representations and reconstructing outputs through pretrained autoencoders. Although computationally effective, this formulation makes output fidelity dependent on latent compression and reconstruction. Recent advances revisit diffusion directly in pixel space. JiT ( Li and He, 2026 ) demonstrates effective clean-image prediction with plain transformers, while PixelDiT ( Yu et al., 2026b ) combines patch-level and pixel-level processing for efficient pixel-space generation. Complementing these approaches, PiD ( Lu et al., 2026 ) introduces a latent-conditioned pixel diffusion decoder that jointly performs decoding and spatial upsampling, replacing conventional VAE decoding. We build on this pretrained decoder and adapt it from image synthesis to monocular depth estimation. Specifically, depth-aware features learned through latent diffusion adaptation condition pixel-space depth generation, allowing us to reuse pretrained generative knowledge for efficient, high-resolution geometric prediction. 3 Method 3.1 Preliminaries: Flow Matching Flow matching learns a time-dependent velocity field that transports a noise distribution to a target data distribution ( Lipman et al., 2022 ) . Given a clean sample 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} and Gaussian noise ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝑰 ) \bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}) , linear interpolation defines the state and target velocity at time t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] : 𝒙 t = ( 1 − t ) ​ 𝒙 0 + t ​ ϵ , 𝒖 t = d ​ 𝒙 t d ​ t = ϵ − 𝒙 0 , \bm{x}_{t}=(1-t)\bm{x}_{0}+t\bm{\epsilon},\qquad\bm{u}_{t}=\frac{\mathrm{d}\bm{x}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\bm{\epsilon}-\bm{x}_{0}, (1) with t = 0 t=0 denoting the data endpoint and t = 1 t=1 the noise endpoint. Previous studies ( He et al., 2025a ; He et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) have shown that generative depth estimation models benefit from using RGB images as inputs rather than noise and can produce accurate predictions in a single forward pass. In line with these findings, we adopt a single-step flow matching formulation that treats the RGB input 𝒙 rgb \bm{x}_{\mathrm{rgb}} as the state 𝒙 t ⋆ \bm{x}_{t^{\star}} at a fixed timestep t ⋆ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) t^{\star}\in(0,1) . Figure 2: Method overview. (a) An adapted latent predictor, trained with a pixel-space loss, estimates a coarse depth latent from a downsampled RGB image. (b) Conditioned on this latent, the pixel diffusion decoder generates a high-resolution depth map with fine-grained details. (c) A lightweight continuity-promoting module mitigates discontinuity artifacts at patch boundaries. 3.2 Framework Overview We aim to produce detailed, high-resolution depth maps, which requires capturing both scene-wide depth relationships and fine local geometry. Pretrained latent diffusion models combine rich visual priors with compact latent-space modeling. However, spatial compression and autoencoder reconstruction can lose fine details, and high-resolution VAE decoding incurs substantial computational and memory overhead. To address these limitations, we draw on the fine-detail modeling capabilities of pixel diffusion. Specifically, we adapt a pixel diffusion decoder pretrained for image synthesis, PiD ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , to decode coarse depth latents predicted by a depth-adapted latent diffusion model. During decoding, the pixel model uses high-resolution RGB observations to recover depth details beyond the coarse representation, producing a detailed depth map at the target resolution. Figure 2 illustrates the overall framework of our proposed method. Given a high-resolution RGB image 𝒙 rgb H ∈ ℝ H × W × 3 \bm{x}_{\mathrm{rgb}}^{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} , we resize it to a lower resolution (i.e., 512 2 512^{2} pixels in total) and encode it using the pretrained autoencoder encoder ℰ \mathcal{E} . The adapted diffusion transformer v θ v_{\theta} predicts the latent velocity, which is used to obtain a coarse depth latent through a single flow update: 𝒛 rgb L = ℰ ⁡ ( ℛ L ​ ( 𝒙 rgb H ) ) , 𝒛 ^ depth L = 𝒛 rgb L − t ⋆ ​ v θ ​ ( 𝒛 rgb L , t ⋆ ) , \bm{z}_{\mathrm{rgb}}^{L}=\mathcal{E}\!\left(\mathcal{R}_{L}(\bm{x}_{\mathrm{rgb}}^{H})\right),\qquad\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mathrm{depth}}^{L}=\bm{z}_{\mathrm{rgb}}^{L}-t^{\star}v_{\theta}(\bm{z}_{\mathrm{rgb}}^{L},t^{\star}), (3) where ℛ L \mathcal{R}_{L} denotes low-resolution resizing, t ⋆ t^{\star} is a fixed flow timestep ( t ⋆ = 0.5 t^{\star}=0.5 in our method), and 𝒛 rgb L , 𝒛 ^ depth L ∈ ℝ h L × w L × C z \bm{z}_{\mathrm{rgb}}^{L},\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mathrm{depth}}^{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{h_{L}\times w_{L}\times C_{z}} denote the RGB and depth latents, respectively. The pixel diffusion decoder then decodes the predicted coarse depth latent into a high-resolution depth map. Our pixel decoder backbone, PiD, builds on a pixel diffusion PixelDiT ( Yu et al., 2026b ) , which uses diffusion transformer (DiT) blocks to process patch-level features and pixel transformer (PiT) blocks to refine pixel-level details. PiD interpolates the latents to be decoded to the target patch grid of size H / p × W / p H/p\times W/p and injects them into the DiT blocks through a lightweight convolutional adapter and gated feature addition, where p p denotes the patch size. We retain this conditioning architecture, replacing the image latent with the predicted coarse depth latent and using the original high-resolution RGB image 𝒙 rgb H \bm{x}_{\mathrm{rgb}}^{H} as the pixel diffusion input state. We further insert a continuity-promoting module before the final linear projection to reduce patch-boundary artifacts in the predicted depth. The resulting decoder predicts high-resolution depth in a single step: 𝒙 ^ depth H = Π ⁡ [ f ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 rgb H , t ⋆ , 𝒛 ^ depth L ) ] ∈ ℝ H × W , \hat{\bm{x}}_{\mathrm{depth}}^{H}=\Pi\!\left[f_{\phi}\!\left(\bm{x}_{\mathrm{rgb}}^{H},t^{\star},\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mathrm{depth}}^{L}\right)\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W}, (4) where f ϕ f_{\phi} is the pixel diffusion decoder and Π \Pi represents averaging the three output channels into a single depth map. This coarse-to-fine design enables efficient high-resolution depth prediction with accurate scene-level structure and fine geometric detail. 3.3 Adapting Latent Diffusion for Coarse Depth Prediction Accurate coarse depth provides reliable geometric guidance for subsequent detail refinement, motivating us to improve the accuracy of the latent depth predictor. Prior works have established effective strategies for adapting pretrained generative models to depth estimation ( Ke et al., 2024a ; He et al., 2025a ; He et al., 2025b ) . Motivated by these findings, we adopt deterministic single-step prediction and replace noise inputs with encoded RGB images. We use FLUX.2-klein-4B ( Black Forest Labs, 2026 ) , a pretrained rectified-flow transformer, as our backbone to balance model capability and computational efficiency. To improve accuracy, we revisit the supervision objective for the latent predictor. Conventional latent flow matching trains models to predict instantaneous velocities in latent space. However, flow trajectories are not necessarily straight, so even accurate instantaneous velocities may yield endpoint errors in a single-step update ( Frans et al., 2025 ) . Moreover, although latent-space supervision encourages predictions to match targets, the decoder may still amplify small residual errors. Thus, latent-space supervision may be suboptimal. Since our single-step formulation does not require iterative latent-space sampling, we can directly supervise the decoded depth map: 𝒙 ^ depth L = Π ⁡ [ 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝒛 ^ depth L ) ] , ℒ coarse = ℒ depth ​ ( 𝒙 ^ depth L , 𝒙 depth L ) , \hat{\bm{x}}_{\mathrm{depth}}^{L}=\Pi\!\left[\mathcal{D}\!\left(\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mathrm{depth}}^{L}\right)\right],\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{coarse}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{depth}}\!\left(\hat{\bm{x}}_{\mathrm{depth}}^{L},\bm{x}_{\mathrm{depth}}^{L}\right), (5) where 𝒟 \mathcal{D} denotes the VAE decoder, Π \Pi averages the output channels, 𝒙 depth L \bm{x}_{\mathrm{depth}}^{L} is the normalized low-resolution ground-truth depth, and ℒ depth \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{depth}} denotes the loss used for depth supervision. We freeze the decoder and backpropagate the depth loss through it, training the latent predictor under a fixed decoding mapping. This objective evaluates the quality of latent predictions by the accuracy of their decoded depth maps, encouraging accurate depth values and geometric structure. 3.4 Decoding Fine-Grained Depth with Pixel Diffusion Central to our approach is adapting a pretrained pixel diffusion decoder to depth estimation. Compared with a conventional VAE decoder trained for reconstruction, a pixel diffusion decoder provides a generative prior learned in pixel space that can help recover fine details beyond the coarse latent representation. Specifically, we build upon PiD ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , which formulates latent decoding as latent-conditioned image generation in pixel space. While the original model decodes natural-image latents, we fine-tune it to decode the predicted coarse depth latents into detailed, high-resolution depth maps using the high-resolution RGB input, as described in Section 3.2 . Following prior findings on pixel-space diffusion ( Li and He, 2026 ) , we use direct clean-sample prediction (x-pred). To initialize the x-pred decoder from PiD’s pretrained velocity model, we negate the weights and bias of its final linear layer: the negated velocity target, − 𝒖 t = 𝒙 0 − ϵ -\bm{u}_{t}=\bm{x}_{0}-\bm{\epsilon} , differs from the clean-sample target 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} only by a noise term. The unpatchification head in diffusion transformers maps each patch token to a p × p p\times p pixel block without local spatial mixing, leaving discontinuities along patch boundaries. In depth maps, these artifacts can be especially noticeable at object boundaries, where one patch spans sharply different depths. Convolutions can mitigate these inconsistencies through local feature fusion ( He et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . However, the large patch size in pixel diffusion makes it costly for convolutional heads to capture patch-wide context after unpatchification. We therefore insert a continuity-promoting module before the original output projection, interleaving progressive unpatchification with small-kernel convolutions to mix hidden features at multiple spatial scales. (6) Each step doubles the spatial grid dimensions until the full pixel resolution is reached. The original linear projection is then applied to produce the output. Each Conv–GELU–Conv block is jointly initialized to implement an identity mapping, preserving the pretrained readout at initialization. 3.5 Training Strategy We train the two components sequentially. We then freeze this model and fine-tune PiD at approximately 1024 2 1024^{2} pixels, adapting its pretrained generative prior to decode the predicted depth latents and recover fine geometric details with RGB guidance. The latent branch predicts coarse depth latents from downsampled RGB inputs, while the pixel branch generates depth directly at the target resolution conditioned on these latents. This design retains learned geometric priors while reducing detail loss from latent-space modeling and VAE reconstruction. It also avoids the substantial overhead of VAE decoding at high resolutions. We train two variants: one at approximately 1024 2 1024^{2} pixels and a mixed-resolution extension supporting prediction up to 4K ( 2160 × 3840 2160\times 3840 ). Experiments on five commonly used depth estimation datasets and Synth4K demonstrate strong overall accuracy and better preservation of fine structures and object boundaries.
